name: Argobba
confidence_why: No description of Argobba itself (Leslau 1959, Leslau 1997, Hudson 1997, Voigt 2003, Getahun Amare 2017 and 2025, Mitike Asrat 2010) says anything about word stress, and the only relevant statement, Leslau's family-wide remark (1951, 1966) that Ethiopic word stress is weak or absent in isolated words, does not name Argobba, so the record is an extrapolation from the family rather than a finding about the language.

Bryan (eds.), Linguistic Analyses: The Non-Bantu Languages of North-Eastern Africa, 593-613. London: OUP; reprinted in Leslau, Wolf. 1988. The Semitic Languages, 457-485; Voigt 2003 Encyclopaedia Aethiopica 1: 330-331; Getahun Amare 2017, 2025; Mitike Asrat 2010.
catalog_locator: Leslau 1988 reprint (archive.org item leslau-fifty-years-of-research-1988): 1966 §1.8 'Stress' at reprint p. 157; 1951 §2 'The accent in the perfect' at reprint p. 229 (page marker '229' follows the footnotes).
catalog_quote: 1. 8. Stress In most of the ETHIOPIC languages Stress is not easily perceptible in the word. In GEʿEZ, HARARI, and CHAHA the penultimate seems normally to be stressed. [Leslau 1966, reprint p. 157] ... 2. The accent in the perfect The isolated forms and words have no stress in Ethiopic in general. Geez alone seems to show some principles for the stress according to the traditional pronunciation, although there is no consistency in the various studies dealing with the subject. Concerning the 3rd person of the perfect there is general agreement, namely, that the penult syllable is stressed, thus nägä́rä. The only South Ethiopic language which also has the penult syllable stressed is the perfect in Harari, thus säbára. [Leslau 1951, reprint p. 229]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

File (a) 1966 passage at the scanned textdirectly under the running head 'CHARACTERISTICS OF THE ETHIOPIAN LANGUAGES 157' and after §1.7 Assimilation: '1. 8. Stress / In most of the ETHIOPIC languages Stress is not easily perceptible in the word. / In GESEZ, HARARI, and CHAHA the penultimate seems normally to be stressed.' Verbatim except scanned 'GESEZ' for GEʿEZ (as the compiler noted). Reprint p. 157 confirmed; the volume's contents list the 'Characteristics' reprint starting at p. 153. §1.7 names ARGOBBA ('any consonant in AMHARIC, ARGOBBA, and TIGRINYA') and §1.6 names ARGOBBA (-c suffix), so Argobba is within the article's scope, but it is not named in…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level statement by Argobba's primary describer: in Ethiopic Semitic generally (Geez, Harari and Chaha excepted, which show penultimate stress) word stress is not easily perceptible / isolated words have no stress. Argobba is covered only by implication (it is one of the South Ethiopic languages the 1966 article treats and is named in the preceding §1.7); no Argobba-specific stress rule exists in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Geez, Harari and Chaha are said to have penultimate stress (Harari in the perfect); Geez only per traditional pronunciation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('in the word', 'isolated forms and words'). Not Argobba-specific: the Argobba-specific descriptions opened (Leslau 1959 sketch, Leslau 1997 grammar phonology chapter, Hudson 1997 handbook chapter, Voigt 2003, Getahun Amare 2017/2025) are all silent on stress. scanned of the 1988 reprint renders GEʿEZ as 'GESEZ'.
new_statements.identity_note: Argobba (argo1244, ISO agj) has several mutually distant varieties. Leslau 1959/1997 describe the Aliyu Amba–Ankober (Shewa) variety, which Leslau calls 'North Argobba' as opposed to the extinct 'South Argobba' of Harar (Cohen 1939); Wetter 2006/2010/2023 and Getahun Amare 2009/2025 describe the archaic Shonke–T'ollaha (Wällo) variety; Zelealem Leyew/Siebert 1994 the Shewa Robit variety. Glottolog 5.1 has no separate codes for these varieties; the family-level Leslau remarks quoted apply to Ethiopic Semitic as a group, not to a named Argobba variety.

Leslau's own Argobba grammar (1997) is silent on stress: no section, no incidental remark in the complete phonology chapter, nothing in the table of contents. This neither confirms nor refutes the 'no word stress' inheritance from the Ethiopic-wide remark.
